title: What would actually happen if you stepped onto Mars without a suit?
description:
Step onto Mars without a suit and your blood won't boil, but the saliva on your tongue will. Mars' air is under 1% of Earth's pressure, low enough for water to boil at body temperature; your skin and blood vessels keep your blood under pressure. NASA knows partly from a 1965 vacuum-chamber accident.

Sources:
- Mars Fact Sheet — NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (NSSDCA): https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/marsfact.html
- Earth Fact Sheet — NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (NSSDCA): https://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/planetary/factsheet/earthfact.html
- Mars Facts — NASA Science: https://science.nasa.gov/mars/facts/
- Armstrong limit — Wikipedia: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armstrong_limit
- Ask an Astrophysicist: space travel archive (human exposure to vacuum; the 1965 suit-leak accident) — NASA Goddard Space Flight Center, Imagine the Universe! (HEASARC): https://imagine.gsfc.nasa.gov/ask_astro/space_travel.html
- Human Exposure to the Vacuum of Space — Aerospaceweb.org: https://aerospaceweb.org/question/atmosphere/q0291.shtml

Labels: simplified: Mars (about 0.64 kPa) is not a perfect vacuum, but it is about ten times below the Armstrong limit (6.3 kPa), so for your body we use NASA's vacuum-exposure accounts. The 1965 account (14 seconds, the water on his tongue beginning to boil) is from a scientist at NASA's Manned Spacecraft Center, on NASA's Imagine the Universe! site; the test subject is not drawn. 10 to 15 seconds of consciousness: 1950s-60s decompression research via Aerospaceweb, and NASA.
Drawn in code; narration is a synthetic voice (Kokoro-82M). Music generated with ACE-Step 1.5; sound effects from Kenney (CC0).
